cards.explanation: The answer is: unless the LORD builds it. Solomon, Israel's king, says it straight: "Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain…" Builders can haul and hammer all day, friends, but without Him the work is in vain. I've pressed a lot of dough in my day, and I know the feeling of working hard on something that needed more than me. Solomon puts the LORD at the center of the whole building.

The answer is False. Solomon, Israel's king, says "unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain." The watchmen do their job, friends, but it's the LORD who protects the city. Wide-open eyes can't do what He does.

The answer is sleep. "…for He gives sleep to His beloved." That's the end of verse 2. Solomon, Israel's king, says rising early and staying up late, toiling for bread to eat, is in vain, and then he names what He gives to His beloved: sleep. A whole verse about working, friends, and it lands on a pillow.
The answer is: from the LORD. "Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD…" That's how verse 3 begins. A heritage is something handed to you, friends. The psalm says the LORD is the One handing it.
The answer is True. Verse 3 says "…the fruit of the womb is His reward." A reward is something given, not something you grab, friends. The psalm says it comes from the LORD.

The answer is blessed. "Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them." That's verse 5, loud and clear. Solomon, Israel's king, has just compared children to arrows, so a full quiver is a good sight to him. The word he picks, friends, is blessed.

The answer is: when he confronts enemies at the gate. The verse says "He will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate." That's the moment Solomon, Israel's king, names. The man with the full quiver is not put to shame there. A gate is a place where the city meets whoever comes.

The answer is: all who fear the LORD. "Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!" That's how this song opens, friends. It's one big blessing before anything else gets said. The word "all" is right there in the text.

The answer is True. The song says "Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!" The second half is how the song describes them: they walk in His ways. They're people who fear the LORD AND walk in His ways, friends.

The answer is blessings and prosperity. Verse 2 says "For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours." It's a gift that comes with the work, friends. Blessings and prosperity, fresh out of the oven if you ask me.

The answer is: it's full of life and growth. A vine that's fruitful and flourishing is a living, growing thing. I think that's the picture, friends: a house with life in it. The song says "Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house…"

The answer is table. The song says "…your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table." It compares the sons to olive shoots, which are young, new growth, and it has them sitting around the table. It's a picture of a family together, friends.

The answer is blessing. "In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD." That's verse 4, and it ties up what came before, friends. It starts with "In this way…" pointing back at the wife, the sons and the table. The word it lands on is blessing.

The answer is the prosperity of Jerusalem. The song says "May the LORD bless you from Zion, that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life…" It's a wish for the whole city's good, friends, not only the family at the table. It starts with "May the LORD bless you from Zion…" so it's a wish.
The answer is True. Verse 6 says "…that you may see your children’s children." That's the wish after Jerusalem's prosperity, friends. The song then closes with "Peace be upon Israel!"
